swap_test.redacted_body: [COMPANY] just posted 8% revenue growth and its first positive Q2 Adjusted EBITDA in four years — a turning point moment your team will want to keep talking about. Your tech blog is the place doing that talking, with deep dives on AI, audio processing, and product innovation like [PRODUCT]'s speech enhancement work. verdicts.notes: Not a template. The argument is load-bearing on three specifics that survive proper-noun redaction — the 8%/first-positive-Q2-EBITDA-in-four-years figure, the documented 1-2 posts/month cadence, and the speech-enhancement deep dive — and none of them transfer to another prospect. The email would have to be rewritten, not find-and-replaced, to send elsewhere. One blocking issue only: the drafter reasoned past its evidence in the third and fourth sentences, inventing an unpublished engineering backlog that no claim supports. It is a plausible inference and that is exactly why it is dangerous — it reads like a researched observation. Everything mechanical is clean: body 114 words (in 120±10), account brief 228 (in 200-300), subject 44 chars, one ask, no banned phrases, 'What I don't know' present with four genuinely useful unknowns. The pre-check appears to be doing its job; nothing arrived here that code should have caught. This is a one-fix retry — remove or hypothesis-frame the backlog assertion and restore the c4 hedge and it should clear 8.

flags.location: genuinely technical, well-regarded content [c5]
flags.remediation: Delete "well-regarded". Claim c5 establishes only that the tech blog exists and covers AI, Arc Ultra Speech Enhancement, neural networks, and technical deep-dives. It says nothing about how the content is received. A reputational assertion carrying a [c5] tag implies evidence of reception that the brief does not contain, and a rep reading this brief will repeat it on a call. Either cut the adjective or replace with something c5 actually supports (e.g. "technically substantive").

flags.location: that gap could matter more as new products launch and buyers look for technical proof points. Faster research synthesis and drafting could help the blog keep pace with the company's momentum instead of trailing it by weeks.
flags.remediation: These two sentences (~47 of 116 words) are portable boilerplate — they would sit unchanged in an email to any company with an engineering blog. Anchor at least one of them to something Sonos-specific from the brief: a named upcoming launch surface, the Arc Ultra speech-enhancement line of work, or the custom-installer/retail channel from c3 where technical proof points actually get used. Do not add a new factual claim to do it.

swap_test.redacted_body: [COMPANY] posted 8% revenue growth and its first positive Q2 Adjusted EBITDA in four years, what CEO [PERSON] called a turning point for the company. The tech blog already carries real technical depth, publishing on AI, audio processing, and work like [PRODUCT]'s speech enhancement, but it puts out only about one to two posts a month. If engineering output is outpacing what actually gets written up, that gap could matter more as new products launch and buyers look for technical proof points. Faster research synthesis and drafting could help the blog keep pace with the company's momentum instead of trailing it by weeks. Worth a 15-minute call to see if that's actually the bottleneck?

verdicts.notes:
Swap-test call was closer than the false verdict suggests, and I want the human to see the reasoning. The load-bearing specifics that survive proper-noun redaction are numeric: 8% growth, first positive Q2 Adjusted EBITDA in four years, one-to-two posts a month. Strip those and the email collapses into "good quarter, slow blog, we can help" — so it is not a template. But the argument *shape* (financial win + under-published engineering blog) is highly portable, and the back half of the email is where that portability shows. If the drafter keeps reusing this shape across accounts, the swap test will start returning true and I will start blocking on it.

Pipeline issue worth fixing: the Tom Conrad "turning point" line is attributed to [c2], and it appears in the brief's recent_news.summary — but it is absent from the canonical claims[] entry for c2, which stops at the three financial facts. Two different scopes are shipping under one claim_id. I passed it because the brief as a whole is ground truth, but a stricter reviewer or a stricter run would flag it as unsupported and block, which makes verdicts non-reproducible. The researcher should make claims[].statement the single canonical text and have summary fields quote from it rather than extend it.

Also note the account brief's "a pace that suggests either a small team or content taking a back seat to engineering priorities [c4]" — this is inference, not evidence, and it carries a claim tag. It survives only because the very next sentence explicitly says "We don't know whether engineering output actually exceeds what gets published." That hedge is doing real work; if it is ever dropped in a later revision, the sentence becomes blocking drift.

This is attempt 2 and it is close. The single blocking finding is a two-word deletion. I expect attempt 3 to pass.

flags.location: Turning research and engineering notes into drafts faster would let the blog keep pace with launches instead of trailing them by weeks.
flags.remediation: Delete 'instead of trailing them by weeks.' No claim in the brief establishes any relationship between blog publishing timing and product launches — the account brief itself lists 'How blog publishing is timed relative to product launches' as an open unknown. Either cut the clause and end the sentence at 'keep pace with launches,' or reframe it as a question rather than an assertion (e.g. 'if the blog is running behind launches, that gap is usually a drafting-speed problem'). Do not assert publishing lag as fact.

flags.location: That same technical detail is what the custom installers and retail partners carrying Sonos across more than 50 countries need to sell new products with confidence [c3].
flags.remediation: c3 supports the distribution channel and the 50-country figure only. It does not support a claim about what those partners need in order to sell. Hedge the inference so the citation covers only the verifiable half — e.g. 'Sonos sells through custom installers and retail partners in more than 50 countries [c3]; that channel usually runs on technical detail.' Keep the assertion visibly the sender's opinion, not sourced fact.

flags.location: a turning point per CEO Tom Conrad [c2]
flags.remediation: The Conrad attribution appears in the brief's recent_news summary under c2 but not in the c2 claim statement itself. It survives, but keep the 'per CEO Tom Conrad' attribution intact on any rewrite — do not restate 'turning point' as the drafter's own characterization of the quarter.

swap_test.redacted_body: [COMPANY] just posted [N]% revenue growth and its first positive Q2 Adjusted EBITDA in four years, a turning point per CEO [PERSON]. Its tech blog already covers real engineering work, including [PRODUCT]'s speech-enhancement processing and other technical deep dives on audio processing and machine learning, but ships only about [N] posts a month. That same technical detail is what the custom installers and retail partners carrying [COMPANY] across more than [N] countries need to sell new products with confidence. Turning research and engineering notes into drafts faster would let the blog keep pace with launches instead of trailing them by weeks. Worth a 15-minute call to see if that's actually the bottleneck?

verdicts.notes:
Swap test passes but not comfortably. The load-bearing specifics are the speech-enhancement deep dive (without it, 'covers real engineering work' is an empty compliment) and the custom-installer/retail channel, which is the one argument here that would not transfer to a typical SaaS target. Sentences 4 and 5 are fully portable and would survive on any company. If a future attempt loses the channel sentence, re-run this check hard — the remaining email is a template.

Pipeline observation, not a document problem: this is attempt 3, and the failure is the drafter asserting in the email something it explicitly lists as unknown in its own account_brief.what_i_dont_know. That is mechanically detectable. Recommend a pre-check that cross-references email body assertions against the what_i_dont_know entries and rejects before it reaches review — it would have caught this and attempt 2's likely equivalent without burning a QA cycle. Constraints were otherwise clean on arrival (body 116, brief 262, subject 34 chars, single ask, no banned phrases), so the upstream code gate is working for what it covers.

email.subject: how Notion decides what gets a hero image
email.body: Notion's "What's New" page runs on a clear structure: major features get hero-image blog posts, minor ones get folded into monthly roundups [c4]. verdicts.notes:
Swap test was borderline and I want the human to see my reasoning rather than just the boolean. The opening frame ("your What's New page runs on a clear structure: major features get hero images, minor ones get roundups") would transfer verbatim to Linear, Figma, Vercel, or any other changelog publisher using the same pattern. What saves it is that the hero/roundup split is a researched observation with a source (c4, c5) rather than an assumption, and the closing ask is built specifically on the sorting decision that split creates — remove the split and there is no email left. Ruled not-a-template, but a drafter who wants a comfortable margin should anchor the opener to something only this page does.

Pipeline issue worth fixing upstream: the research brief attaches claim_id c5 to a marketing_task block whose why_ai_helps field contains a quantitative assertion ("15+ features per month") that does not appear in the c5 claim statement. That structure invites exactly the drift flagged here — the drafter cited in good faith and still ended up asserting an unsourced number. Recommend either (a) the researcher promotes any figure appearing in marketing_task to its own entry in claims[] with a source, or (b) the drafter contract states explicitly that marketing_task.why_ai_helps is analyst inference and not citable. This will recur across accounts otherwise.

Code-checked constraints all clean on arrival: body 114 words (in range even after excluding the five [cN] tokens), subject 41 chars, account brief 213 words, one ask, "What I don't know" present with four substantive entries, no banned phrases. Pre-check has no hole I can see.

One retry should clear this. The email is structurally sound and the opener carries real information; the only blocking issue is a single number that needs to be sourced or removed.

flags.location: Worth 15 minutes to see if that stage could run smoother?
flags.remediation: The CTA is time-boxed but the email never states what the sender actually does. A reader finishes this with no idea what 'run smoother' means in practice or who is offering it. Add one clause naming the concrete offer (e.g. what the sender would show or do in those 15 minutes) so the ask points at something specific rather than at an unnamed improvement.

flags.location: the kind of moment when marketing needs to look sharp fast, not scramble
flags.remediation: This is an inferred-pressure trope that attaches to any recently-funded company and does no work here — it never connects the tender offer or revenue growth to the release-notes cadence that the rest of the email is about. Either cut the funding/revenue sentence and reinvest the ~25 words in the release-notes observation, or make the connection explicit and non-generic.

flags.location: When the sorting and drafting step moves faster, there's more room to get each post right instead of racing the calendar.
flags.remediation: Content-free value hypothesis: it does not say what changes, who does it, or what 'faster' looks like. Replace with a specific statement about the sorting or drafting step, or delete it and give the words to the ask.

flags.remediation: Not blocking — this traces to the brief's own marketing_task wording ('minor improvements get monthly roundups with visual hierarchy'). But c5's underlying statement attaches 'narrative and visual hierarchy' to the dedicated blog posts, not the roundups. Tighten to what c4/c5 assert directly (major features get hero-image posts; minor improvements get grouped into monthly roundups) rather than importing the visual-hierarchy attribute onto the roundup.

Pipeline observation rather than document observation: this is attempt 2 and both attempts have produced a CTA with no stated offer. The email spends 25 of 120 words on funding/revenue that never connect to the release-notes thesis, then runs out of room to say what the sender does. verdicts.notes:
Provenance is clean. Every factual assertion in the body traces to c4/c5 and is restated without inflation — notably the drafter declined to import the '15+ features per month' figure from marketing_task.why_ai_helps (which is task framing, not a claim) and instead logged it under what_i_dont_know as needing confirmation. That is the correct handling and worth reinforcing upstream; earlier attempts in this run appear to have been where that number was tested.

Swap-test call, since it is the disputable one: redacted, the email loses its entire argument. The body is 78 of 118 words describing one observed editorial structure, and the ask is a direct function of that structure. It reads as coherent English but not as a sendable email — 'your [PAGE] splits [OUTPUT] into two tracks' is only meaningful if that structure is verifiably true of the recipient, and it is not true of most SaaS release blogs, which run a flat changelog. I record this as passing, but flag for the human that the specificity here sits at the category level (SaaS release-notes practice) rather than at something only Notion does. A stricter reviewer could rule the other way. If this account converts to a template across other targets, that is the signal that the swap test was too lenient here.

Constraints all clean on arrival — body 118 words plus 3 citation tokens against a 110–130 band, subject 37 chars, brief 232 words, one ask, what_i_dont_know populated with five substantive entries including two epistemic hedges. No evidence of a pre-check hole in this run.

Pipeline note: this is attempt 3 and it lands exactly at the gate. The retry loop did its job, but three attempts to reach a bare pass suggests the drafter's first-pass instructions are under-specifying the closing ask — both remaining flags are in the last two sentences, and both are the kind of thing a drafter fixes in one edit if told the ask must state its duration exactly once and must not use blank-page framing.
